The pronoun **him** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and I struck them]

Yahweh is describing one event, **I hid**, before describing another event that preceded it, **I was angry**. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [I was angry, so I hid]

Yahweh is using **I hid** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I withdrew my favor from the people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I withdrew my favor]

Yahweh is speaking of the people (in the singular) persisting in their own rebellious desires as if a person **went backward in the way of his heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he kept following his own rebellious desires]

x.ASV: I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners.
x.Darby: I have seen his ways, and will heal him; and I will lead him, and will restore comforts unto him and to those of his that mourn.
x.KJV: I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners.
x.YLT: His ways I have seen, and I heal him, yea, I lead him, And recompense comforts to him and to his mourning ones.

nt: Yahweh uses the word **and** here to indicate a contrast between the people’s sinful ways and his decision to heal and restore them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I have seen his ways. Nevertheless, I will heal him]

Yahweh is speaking of restoring the people to well-being as if he would **heal** a sick person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will restore him to well-being]

x.ASV: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him that is far off and to him that is near, saith Jehovah; and I will heal him.
x.Darby: I create the fruit of the lips: peace, peace to him [that is] afar off, and to him [that is] nigh, saith Jehovah; and I will heal him.
x.KJV: I create the fruit of the lips; Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the Lord; and I will heal him.
x.YLT: Producing the fruit of the lips, `Peace, peace,' to the far off, and to the near, And I have healed him, said Jehovah.

nt: Here, **the lips** represents what a person says, in this case words of praise. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the praise that people speak]

Yahweh is repeating the word **peace** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Complete peace]

Yahweh is referring to all people by naming two extremes, **the faraway** and **the near**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to everyone everywhere]

x.ASV: But the wicked are like the troubled sea; for it cannot rest, and its waters cast up mire and dirt.
x.Darby: But the wicked are like the troubled sea, which cannot rest, and whose waters cast up mire and dirt.
x.KJV: But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.
x.YLT: And the wicked are as the driven out sea, For to rest it is not able, And its waters cast out filth and mire.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **the driven sea** cannot rest and keeps churning up mud, so **the wicked** find no peace and continually produce evil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [But the wicked will find no peace, just as the driven sea keeps churning]

Yahweh is using the plural adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean people of a certain kind. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [But wicked people]

x.ASV: There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.
x.Darby: There is no peace, saith myGod, to the wicked.
x.KJV: There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.
x.YLT: There is no peace, said my God, to the wicked!

nt: Here Isaiah marks these words as a direct quotation of what Yahweh says. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [My God says that there is no peace for the wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Nothing will be well]
